arlington-heights.water_system: Village of Arlington Heights operates its own municipal water system; Lake Michigan water since 1985 via the Northwest Water Commission, which receives water treated at the City of Evanston plant (poly orthophosphate corrosion inhibitor added there); deep wells kept only as backup
arlington-heights.program_name: Residential Lead Line Replacement Program (also referenced as the Lead Service Line Replacement Project for village-led construction work)
arlington-heights.cost_coverage: Homeowner pays for the private-side replacement at their own expense through a New Water Service permit (which "may qualify for a no fee permit"), then after the work is complete may apply for reimbursement of the lesser of 50% or $2,500, depending on funds available each year; no payment plan or water-bill financing option is mentioned on the Village's lead information page.
arlington-heights.homeowner_cost: Homeowner pays for the private-side replacement up front, then applies for reimbursement of the lesser of 50% or $2,500, subject to available annual funding; the required New Water Service permit may qualify for a no-fee permit. No payment plan or water-bill financing option is mentioned on the Village's lead information page.
arlington-heights.how_to_check_line: Official GIS Water Service Material Map: https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/cbf93ed7e7994c3f83575431f7ada5b4/ ; the Village page also gives a key/coin-and-magnet self-test method, or residents can contact Village staff. Project-specific locations are on the Village interactive map under the "Water and Wastewater" tab.
arlington-heights.how_to_apply: For private-side reimbursement: (1) obtain a New Water Service permit from the Building & Life Safety Department (may qualify for no-fee permit), (2) complete the replacement at own expense, (3) apply for reimbursement based on available annual funding. Contact for the village-led replacement project: Public Works & Engineering Department, Scott Schweda, 847-368-5800.
arlington-heights.notes: Village-led Lead Service Line Replacement Project (contractor Miller Pipeline, engineering by Engineering Enterprises, Inc.) is scheduled Spring 2026 to Fall 2026, funded from the Capital Improvement Program Fund; the Village communicates directly with residents via flyer or door hanger before working in an area. Public-side work is coordinated with major capital projects first. The Village's Initial LSL Replacement Plan (PDF on vah.com) targets replacing 6% of LSLs per year beginning 2027 with a schedule running through 2043 under the Illinois Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act. The Village states its water supply has "consistently tested safe" and complies with all federal and state standards. Galvanized service lines are included as eligible for the replacement incentive per the program guidelines.

barrington.water_system: Village of Barrington operates its own community water system; the Public Works page states the Village provides water services to residents and businesses in Barrington and portions of neighboring communities. Lead is stated as NOT found in the Village's water source or treated drinking water; polyphosphates are added to prevent lead leaching from pipes.
barrington.program_name: not named (Village pages refer to it as the Lead Water Service Line Replacement program, undertaken pursuant to the Illinois Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act of August 2021)
barrington.cost_coverage: The Village "has secured grant funding from the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency to help cover the cost of the replacement program, which will come at no cost to any individual homeowner." The pages do not break the coverage down into public vs. private portions.
barrington.homeowner_cost: $0 — "no cost to any individual homeowner" per the Village's official lead service line replacement pages.
barrington.how_to_check_line: Official online inventory/map of lead and copper water service lines for all residential, commercial, and institutional properties (ArcGIS viewer): https://barrington-il.maps.arcgis.com/apps/View/index.html?appid=e515cd497a60499d9c1ea3c411eb2fa7. Village notes structures built prior to 1986 may have a lead service line.
barrington.how_to_apply: No application form is published. Residents are directed to contact the Village Public Works Department: water@barrington-il.gov, (847) 304-3362 (general Public Works: vobpw@barrington-il.gov, (847) 381-7903).
barrington.notes: Village is required by the Illinois Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act (signed August 2021) to inventory service line materials, report findings to the State, and present a long-range replacement plan. Funding is via IEPA grant. The official web pages read do not publish phase details, timelines, waitlists, or coordination with water-main projects (a $4M IEPA forgivable loan / Phase I figure of 210 of ~660 lead lines replaced appears in search summaries attributed to Village materials, including a State of the Village PDF that could not be parsed, but was not verifiable on the official pages actually read — treat as unconfirmed). Village states lead is not present in its source or treated water and that it meets all IEPA requirements including polyphosphate corrosion control.

barrington-hills.water_system: Barrington Hills has NO municipal water system. The Village's official page states: "The Village does not provide water and sewer services for its residents" — most homes are on private wells (and septic). However, the neighboring Village of Barrington states officially: "The Village provides residents and businesses in Barrington and portions of Inverness and Barrington Hills with water and sewer services" — so a small portion of Barrington Hills is on Barrington's community water system, and Barrington's lead program applies to those addresses.
barrington-hills.program_name: not named (Barrington Hills has no program of its own; the Village of Barrington's "Lead Service Line Replacement Program" covers the portions of Barrington Hills on Barrington water)
barrington-hills.cost_coverage: Barrington Hills itself: not published (no water utility, no program). For addresses served by the Village of Barrington: Barrington's official lead service line page states the Village secured Illinois EPA grant funding for the replacement program "which will come at no cost to any individual homeowner." Barrington also notes state funding is extremely limited and distributed first-come-first-served.
barrington-hills.homeowner_cost: For Barrington-water customers (including the served portions of Barrington Hills): $0 — "no cost to any individual homeowner" per the Village of Barrington. For the majority of Barrington Hills homes on private wells: not applicable/not published (the Illinois LSLR Act's inventory/replacement requirements apply to community water systems, not private wells).
barrington-hills.how_to_check_line: Barrington Hills publishes nothing (private wells have no utility service line inventory). For homes on Barrington water: the Village of Barrington provides an online inventory/interactive ArcGIS map of lead and copper water service lines on its Lead Water Service Line Replacement page; structures built before 1986 may have lead service lines.
barrington-hills.how_to_apply: No Barrington Hills process exists. For Barrington-water addresses: contact Village of Barrington Public Works — water@barrington-il.gov / (847) 304-3362, or vobpw@barrington-il.gov / (847) 304-3368; the Village requests resident participation/support to qualify for state funding. No formal application form is published.
barrington-hills.notes: Barrington Hills (distinct from the Village of Barrington) is a rural large-lot community: its official pages say most residences use private wells and septic, recommend annual private well water testing through the Barrington Area Council of Governments (BACOG) or county health departments, and contain no mention of lead service lines at all. Lead-in-water risk management there is the homeowner's responsibility via well testing, not a utility replacement program. The only municipal LSLR program touching the village is Barrington's IEPA-grant-funded, no-cost-to-homeowner program (Barrington received IEPA lead service line replacement funding and filed a Project Plan in Oct 2020), applicable solely to the portions of Barrington Hills connected to Barrington's water system. Funding is first-come-first-served per Barrington; no timeline or waitlist details are published.

buffalo-grove.water_system: Village of Buffalo Grove operates its own water system (IEPA system ID IL0314180, ~12,149 service lines); source water is Lake Michigan purchased through the Northwest Water Commission ("Buffalo Grove purchases the water from the Northwest Water Commission").
buffalo-grove.cost_coverage: not published — no replacement program exists because the Village's IEPA-filed 2026 Final Material Inventory reports Total Lead: 0, Total Galvanized Requiring Replacement: 0, Total Unknown: 0 out of 12,149 total service lines (all 12,149 classified Non-Lead). The Village FAQ states "we have no known lead service lines in the Village," while noting lead lines "have occasionally been found during Village maintenance and construction work."
buffalo-grove.homeowner_cost: not published (no replacement program; note the Village states general service-line maintenance/repair from the main to the house, including the b-box, is the homeowner's responsibility)
buffalo-grove.how_to_check_line: Official Water Quality page (vbg.org/583/Water-Quality) links the Village's Service Line Inventory file (IEPA 2026 Final Material Inventory) and an interactive Water Service Line ArcGIS dashboard map (arcgis.com/apps/dashboards/cbd6bca891ec48c7b81693eea57e6e44); residents can also contact Public Works at 847-459-2545.
buffalo-grove.how_to_apply: not published (no program to apply to); water/lead questions go to Public Works / Superintendent of Water Operations, 847-459-2545
buffalo-grove.notes: Buffalo Grove is effectively a "no lead lines" community under the Illinois LSLRNA: its April 2026 IEPA inventory shows zero lead, zero galvanized-requiring-replacement, and zero unknown lines, so no replacement plan or village cost-share program is posted. Residents near construction receive IEPA-required lead-precaution letters ("The letter is a requirement of the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency") because disturbance can affect lead content even in non-lead systems. Standard service lines are described as copper from the corporation stop at the main, through the b-box, to the in-home meter. The 2024 Consumer Confidence Report (CCR-2024 PDF) is published but its text was not machine-readable; findings above come from the FAQ, Water Quality page, Getting Water to your Home page, and the inventory spreadsheet itself.

chicago.water_system: City of Chicago's own system — the Department of Water Management (DWM) treats Lake Michigan water at the City's water treatment plants and delivers it citywide; Lead-Safe Chicago (leadsafechicago.org) is the City's official lead program portal.
chicago.program_name: Lead-Safe Chicago — Lead Service Line Replacement programs: Equity LSLR Program, Homeowner-Initiated Program, Breaks and Leaks Replacement Program, Block-Long Replacement Program (plus a Daycare LSLR Program)
chicago.cost_coverage: $0 to the homeowner under the Equity, Breaks and Leaks, and Block-Long programs. Equity Program: City covers the full cost — "a free lead service line replacement all the way from the water main into your home plus installation of a free water meter" (a $16,000–$30,000 value) — for owner-occupant homeowners with household income below 80% of area median income; program size is limited by available funding and requires an application. Breaks and Leaks: if your line breaks or leaks it is mandatory to call 311, and the City replaces "both the private and public sides of the line for free" (per state law effective January 2023 banning partial replacements). Block-Long: when the City performs scheduled maintenance on aging water or sewer mains, lead service lines impacted by that work are replaced for free. Homeowner-Initiated Program: the homeowner pays their own licensed contractor (contractor cost not published by the City); the City waives permit fees — stated as savings of up to $3,100 in the program details, though another section of the same page says up to $5,000 (additional permits/fees from other agencies such as IDOT may still apply) — connects the new line to the water main, and provides a free water meter if one is not already in place. The fee waiver applies only to standalone replacements, not those done as part of a home renovation or expansion.
chicago.homeowner_cost: $0 under the Equity, Breaks and Leaks, and Block-Long programs. Under the Homeowner-Initiated Program the homeowner pays the licensed plumber/contractor; the City waives permit fees (up to $3,100) and provides a free meter and free connection to the main. Dollar figures for the homeowner's contractor cost are not published.
chicago.how_to_check_line: Official citywide Service Line Inventory lookup at sli.chicagowaterquality.org (map-based: navigate to your address and click to see your service line material, covering both the private portion from the b-box to the building and the public portion from the b-box to the main). Residents can also request a free water lead test kit by calling 311 or via chicagowaterquality.org, and the Homeowner-Initiated page provides a self-check checklist.
chicago.how_to_apply: Equity Program: apply online or download the form at chicagowaterquality.org/LSLREquity; request free water testing via 311. Program contacts published by the City: 312-742-2406 and lead.safe@cityofchicago.org. Homeowner-Initiated: contractor applies for the permit-fee waiver at chicagowaterquality.org/LSLRPermit. Breaks/leaks: report to 311.
chicago.notes: Chicago has roughly 400,000 legacy lead service lines, mostly single-family and two-flat homes — the largest inventory in the US. Equity Program eligibility: own and live in the home, household income below 80% of area median income (page cites $95,900 for a family of 4), with priority for households with children under 18 or elevated lead in free DWM testing; completed applications are processed in the order received (no published timeline). Block-Long replacements are scheduled with the City's water/sewer main projects rather than on request. After replacement the City recommends NSF-53 certified lead-removal filters for the first three months and offers free follow-up testing. The main portal chicago.gov/leadsafechicago pages block automated access; leadsafechicago.org is the same official City program site.

countryside.water_system: City of Countryside operates its own municipal Water Department; water is Lake Michigan water — per the official Water Department page, "a contract was signed with the Village of McCook for the transportation of Lake Michigan water from the City of Chicago."
countryside.cost_coverage: not published — the official Lead Service Line Survey page discusses only the inventory required by the Illinois Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act (Public Act 102-0613), not any replacement program or cost coverage
countryside.how_to_check_line: No public inventory map/portal is published. The city mailed a Lead Service Line Survey to each water customer (June) asking about service line material; residents could return the mailed survey or complete it online via SurveyMonkey. For questions: City Hall / Water Department, 708-354-7270 (service issues 708-354-8827).
countryside.how_to_apply: not published — no replacement/assistance application exists on the official site; contact the Water Department at 708-354-8827 or dkrzebiot@countryside-il.org, 803 Joliet Road, Countryside, IL 60525
countryside.notes: The city's official position, stated verbatim on the Lead Service Line Survey page: "Service lines in our City are mainly copper with a smaller number of galvanized, all of which are not a problem." The page frames the effort purely as the state-mandated material inventory (initial inventory due to Illinois EPA April 15, 2023; complete inventory April 15, 2024) to be turned over to IEPA. No replacement program, timeline, waitlist, loan program, or main-project-coordinated replacement policy is published on countryside-il.org. A newer URL (countryside-il.org/departments/water-department/lead-service-line-survey/) returned 404; the live page is the .php version cited in source_urls.

deer-park.water_system: Deer Park has no municipal water system. Per the Village's official About page: "The water source for most homes is private well. Lake Michigan water is provided in the triangle along the Rand Road corridor." The Village does not name the Lake Michigan supplier on that page, but its official Services Directory lists "Palatine - Water Division" (palatine.il.us/261/Water-Division) as the only water utility, under Governmental Affiliations — indicating the Village of Palatine serves the Rand Road corridor area.
deer-park.program_name: Deer Park itself: not named / no program published. For Palatine-served addresses: "Lead and Galvanized Steel Water Service Line Replacement Cost Sharing Program" (Village of Palatine)
deer-park.cost_coverage: Under Palatine's program: the homeowner hires the contractor and pays the full replacement cost plus permit and inspection fees upfront; the Village reimburses after the work is completed (100% of the water main-to-b-box segment, 75% of the b-box-to-meter segment, up to an $11,000 cap, with permit and inspection fees reimbursable in addition to the cap). The homeowner permanently bears the 25% share of the b-box-to-meter segment and any amount exceeding the $11,000 cap; the homeowner's contractor must restore all disturbed public property to pre-construction condition. For Deer Park's private-well homes: not published (private wells are not part of a public water system).
deer-park.homeowner_cost: Under Palatine's program: homeowner pays permit and inspection fees upfront (reimbursed), plus any cost above the 75% share on the b-box-to-meter segment and any amount exceeding the $11,000 cap; homeowner's contractor must restore disturbed public property. For Deer Park's private-well homes: not published (private wells are not part of a public water system).
deer-park.how_to_check_line: Deer Park publishes no inventory. Palatine customers: (1) address lookup on Palatine's ArcGIS Lead Water Service Inventory dashboard (arcgis.com/apps/dashboards/248b80540e7e468aa3b924e25bb4b6a7); (2) scratch test at the meter (copper = penny-colored non-magnetic, lead = shiny silver non-magnetic, galvanized = dull gray magnetic); (3) email a photo of the meter and adjacent piping to publicworks@palatine.il.us for review.
deer-park.how_to_apply: Via Palatine (if on Palatine water): Department of Public Works Engineering Division, (847) 705-5200, publicworks@palatine.il.us; submit the program application form before obtaining a building permit (application PDF at palatine.il.us/DocumentCenter/View/3072). Deer Park Village Hall for general questions: 847-726-1648. Deer Park itself: not published.
deer-park.notes: Deer Park is a small village with no water utility of its own: most homes are on private wells (the Village's water pages focus on well maintenance, testing, and conservation via the Barrington Area Council of Governments materials), so the Illinois Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act's inventory/replacement obligations largely do not attach to the Village. Only the "triangle along the Rand Road corridor" gets Lake Michigan water, evidently from the Village of Palatine (the sole water utility listed in Deer Park's official Services Directory). Residents in that corridor fall under Palatine's inventory and cost-sharing program; Palatine's pages state eligibility as "all residential properties" with lead/galvanized lines but do not explicitly confirm or exclude Deer Park addresses — affected residents should confirm with Palatine Public Works at (847) 705-5200. No timelines, waitlists, or water-main-coordination details are published on the pages reviewed.

deerfield.water_system: Village of Deerfield operates its own distribution system; water is supplied by the City of Highland Park (Lake Michigan water), which has maintained a corrosion control program since 1992. "Water entering the Village distribution system does not contain lead."
deerfield.program_name: Residential Lead Service Line Replacement Cost Sharing Program (also referred to as "Lead Service Line Replacement Program (LSLR)")
deerfield.cost_coverage: Voluntary residential cost-share (reimbursement) program per the Village's Lead Service Line Replacement Residential Cost Share Program packet (dated February 17, 2026) on deerfield.il.us: for full replacement of the entire lead service line (Village and private portions, water main into the building), the Village reimburses a 50% match up to a maximum of $6,000 per property, and this reimbursement also covers all exterior restoration (roadway, sidewalk, parkway). Where the public portion is known to be copper and only the private portion is lead, reimbursement is a 50% match up to $2,500. Galvanized piping is eligible only when located downstream of lead; only lead portions (plus such galvanized) are eligible. Funding is limited and awarded first-come, first-served; incomplete applications are rejected and forfeit their place in the queue. The program does NOT cover replacements done for repairs, system upgrades, or replacements required by Village ordinance (additions, new construction) or other regulatory agencies, and it is not retroactive — work performed before program approval is not reimbursable. One reimbursement per property; if other private work within 12 months of reimbursement would have required a service replacement anyway, the full reimbursement must be repaid (exception: change of ownership). Ownership context: the Village owns and maintains the portion from the water main up to and including the buffalo box (shutoff valve) or meter pit, typically in the parkway; the property owner owns the portion from the buffalo box into the building. Homeowner cost: the unreimbursed share of costs above the 50% match / cap ($6,000 full, $2,500 private-side-only), plus ineligible items such as interior finishes beyond drywall and basement flooring (e.g., cabinets, shelving), landscaping plantings, and extra costs from a service larger than 1.5-inch or non-metallic pipe. Reimbursement is calculated on a 1.5-inch Type K copper installation. Permit fees typically associated with a water service replacement are waived under the program (street/right-of-way deposits are held for 9 months after restoration acceptance, then released). Many restoration costs ARE reimbursable, including pavement/parkway/lawn restoration, drywall removal, basement flooring removal and replacement, and electrical grounding replacement. The homeowner obtains quotes and hires state-licensed, Village-registered plumbing/electrical contractors; if an outside meter pit exists it must be removed and the meter relocated inside. Reimbursement is paid after completed work, passed inspections, restoration acceptance, and Village approval of the signed Affidavit of Completed Replacement Work (typically mailed within 4-6 weeks).
deerfield.homeowner_cost: The unreimbursed share of costs above the 50% match / reimbursement cap ($6,000 full replacement / $2,500 private-side-only), plus ineligible items such as interior finishes beyond drywall and basement flooring (e.g., cabinets, shelving), landscaping plantings, and extra costs from a service larger than 1.5-inch or non-metallic pipe. Permit fees typically associated with a water service replacement are waived under the program, and many restoration costs (pavement/parkway/lawn restoration, drywall removal, basement flooring removal and replacement, electrical grounding replacement) are reimbursable. Homeowner hires a licensed contractor and pays up front; reimbursement is paid after completed work, passed inspections, and Village approval.
deerfield.how_to_check_line: Village-published Water Service Material Lookup (Community Portal property look-up via GIS Consortium) showing both public and private portions; Village also maintains an inventory based on installation age and building inspection records; self-check instructions (scratch test with key/screwdriver — bright silver indicates lead; magnet test distinguishes galvanized) on the Lead Service Line Information page.
deerfield.how_to_apply: Online application portal via the Village LSLR program page (2025 application opened 9:00 AM March 9, first-come first-served); Program Packet with full requirements linked from deerfield.il.us/990. Contacts: Public Works 847-317-7245, Engineering 847-317-2490.
deerfield.notes: Program is voluntary and demand-limited (first-come, first-served with limited annual funding), not automatically main-project-driven. Village pages note the Illinois Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act (2021) requires municipalities to begin facilitating replacement of known lead service lines starting in 2027. Homes built before ~1960 in Deerfield typically have lead service lines. Galvanized piping is eligible only when located downstream of lead. The 50%/$6,000 and 50%/$2,500 figures appear in the Village's Program Packet PDF (dated February 17, 2026, described as an Administrative Program) linked from the program page. No loan program published.

des-plaines.water_system: City of Des Plaines operates its own water system (IEPA ID IL0310630), purchasing Lake Michigan water from the City of Chicago and the Northwest Water Commission and distributing it to about 18,000 customers. Note: Illinois American Water provides water and sewer service for certain areas of Des Plaines — residents in those areas must contact Illinois American Water directly.
des-plaines.program_name: not named (submitted to IEPA as the City of Des Plaines "Proposed Draft Water Service Line Replacement Plan" / Lead Service Line Replacement Plan, April 2025)
des-plaines.cost_coverage: No direct homeowner charge per the draft plan — the City proposes to bear the entire cost of the project, including the customer's portion, funded from the City's Water Fund; the plan states the Water Fund "can support the project with substantial rate increasing and no financing is proposed" (i.e., costs recovered through water rates), and that "there are no measures to address regarding affordability for customers/ratepayers" and "no need for structuring payments" since the City bears the entire cost. City estimates $21,500 average per service line and $220,719,000 total. Still a proposed draft plan (submitted to IEPA April 15, 2025, watermarked DRAFT).
des-plaines.homeowner_cost: No direct homeowner charge per the draft plan — the City proposes to bear the entire cost including the customer's portion, funded through the Water Fund via "substantial rate increasing" (i.e., recovered through water rates). Still a proposed draft plan.
des-plaines.how_to_check_line: Official Public Service Line Map: https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/fc2a37c34f7b4206b5c44756eed7569c (linked from the 2024 Consumer Confidence Report). The city also publishes its Water Service Line Inventory and Pipe Identification Instructions (self-check of the pipe in the basement between entry point and inlet valve) on desplainesil.gov.
des-plaines.how_to_apply: No application form published. Plan states customers are invited to call Public Works with questions (Public Works and Engineering, 1111 Joseph J. Schwab Rd, Des Plaines, IL 60016, 847-391-5464) or participate at regular City Council meetings (first and third Monday of each month).
des-plaines.notes: Inventory counts per April 2025 draft plan: 16,665 total service lines; 3,431 known lead/galvanized; 6,835 suspected; 51 replaced since 2020. Plan: replace 10,266 lines over 20 years (~514/year; 2,566 by year 5, 5,133 by year 10). The document is a PROPOSED DRAFT plan submitted to Illinois EPA under the Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act — waitlist/scheduling details and coordination with water main projects are not published. City ran a "2023 Lead Service Line Replacement Project" bid. desplainesil.gov blocks direct fetching (Akamai 403); content was obtained via extracted text of the official pages/PDFs.

elgin.water_system: City of Elgin operates its own municipal water system, drawing primarily from the Fox River with supplemental deep wells, treated at two city facilities.
elgin.program_name: Lead Service Line Replacement Program (multi-year city projects, e.g. "YEAR 5 - 2026 Lead Water Service Line Replacement Project")
elgin.cost_coverage: $0 when the replacement is part of a City-initiated project (including the annual Year 3–Year 5 replacement projects, 2024–2026, funded by IEPA and local funds) or an emergency repair such as a water main break or service line leak; for annual-project replacements the owner must opt in by signing a Temporary Construction Easement Acknowledgement Form. If the homeowner initiates the replacement independently, the City pays only the City's portion (water main to the b-box/shutoff valve) and the homeowner pays the private-portion cost (amount not published).
elgin.homeowner_cost: $0 when the replacement is part of a City-initiated project or emergency repair; homeowner pays the private-portion cost only if they initiate the replacement themselves outside a city project (amount not published).
elgin.how_to_check_line: Official online Lead Service Line Map on the city's GIS portal — "To find out if you have a lead service line view this map and search for your address" (linked from elginil.gov/2641/Lead-Service-Lines and ElginIL.gov/lead).
elgin.how_to_apply: City selects and notifies affected property owners by letter each project year; participating owners must sign a Temporary Construction Easement Acknowledgement Form (cityofelgin.org/TCE). Homeowner-initiated replacements require a permit from the Building Division of the Community Development Department. General contact: City of Elgin, 150 Dexter Court, Elgin, IL 60120, 847-931-6001; ElginIL.gov/lead.
elgin.notes: City identified ~13,000 lead service lines in 2018 (~10,000 of ~30,000 total service lines currently lead; ~1,500 unknown-material). Phased annual projects since 2022: Year 3 (2024) ~870 lines (completion May 2025), Year 4 (2025) ~1,000 lines (completion May 2026), Year 5 (2026) ~900 lines, starting summer 2026, expected completion May 2027. Funded by IEPA, Illinois DCEO, congressionally directed spending, and local funds; city replaces the entire service from the water main to the meter inside the property. Replacements are also coordinated with city-funded projects and emergency repairs. City states lead is not present in Elgin's treated drinking water. No waitlist or loan program published.

elk-grove-village.water_system: The Village of Elk Grove Village operates its own community water supply (Illinois EPA facility IL0314400, ~31,800 population served, source type "surface water purchased"). Water is Lake Michigan water treated by the City of Chicago Water Department, delivered via the Northwest Suburban Municipal Joint Action Water Agency (NSMJAWA) reservoirs near O'Hare, then pumped to the Village's distribution system. Emergency interconnections with Arlington Heights, Schaumburg, Bensenville, and Roselle (per Illinois EPA Drinking Water Watch).
elk-grove-village.cost_coverage: not published — the Village's official position is that no program is needed. Official Village statement (news release on Chicago's corrosion-control transition): "Elk Grove Village does not have any lead service lines and as such, this change should have no impact to our water customers" and "Again, Elk Grove Village does not have any lead service lines and as such, this change should have no impact on the water quality in Elk Grove Village—the water in Elk Grove Village remains safe to drink and of the highest quality."
elk-grove-village.homeowner_cost: not published (no lead service lines reported, so no replacement cost framework exists)
elk-grove-village.how_to_check_line: not published — no public service-line inventory map/portal was found on elkgrove.org. The Village publishes annual Water Quality Reports and a "2023 Lead and Copper Report" on its Water Quality Reports page; the Public Works Department (450 E. Devon Ave., 847-734-8800) is the listed water-utility contact.
elk-grove-village.how_to_apply: not published — no application process exists because the Village states it has no lead service lines to replace
elk-grove-village.notes: Key official finding: Elk Grove Village publicly states it has zero lead service lines, so there is no replacement program, cost-sharing policy, or waitlist. The Village statement appeared in an official elkgrove.org news release about the Chicago Department of Water Management's corrosion-control transition (moving to a 30% polyphosphate/70% orthophosphate blend in Dec 2024, reaching 100% orthophosphate by summer 2025), reassuring residents the change has no local impact. Like all Illinois community water supplies, the Village is subject to the Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act (complete material inventory due to IEPA by April 15, 2024); its inventory filings go to IEPA (EPA.LeadandCopper@illinois.gov, 217-785-0561) but IEPA's public page does not display Elk Grove Village's inventory rows. Research caveat: elkgrove.org blocks automated fetching (Akamai 403), so the Village statements above were captured verbatim via search-engine snippets of the official pages rather than a full page render; the Illinois EPA Drinking Water Watch record and IEPA lead-service-line page were fetched and read in full.

elmwood-park.water_system: Village of Elmwood Park operates its own public water supply (IEPA Facility ID IL-0310780); the village's lead hub states "As your water provider, we are doing the following to reduce lead exposure in our water system." Water source (e.g. Lake Michigan purchase) not stated on pages read.
elmwood-park.program_name: Village of Elmwood Park Lead Service Line Replacement Program
elmwood-park.cost_coverage: not published as a resident charge — and the Village's official LSLR Plan (Section 4a) goes further than silence: it states "All replacements will be funded by Village funds, grants and PWSLP funds" and answers "No" to whether the property owner will be responsible for a portion of the replacement cost; the SRF/IEPA-loan-financed project scope runs from the buffalo box to the meter (i.e., includes the private side, budgeted at $10,000 each in village program costs) and residents participate by signing an agreement. Caveat: no page uses the words "free" or "at no cost to the homeowner," and the Plan shows an $88.2M funding shortfall with replacements prioritized (high-risk sites, then streets with water-main projects, then the rest as funding allows), so timing at any individual address is not guaranteed.
elmwood-park.homeowner_cost: not published (no official page states a homeowner charge; the SRF-financed project scope runs from buffalo box to meter and residents participate by signing an agreement)
elmwood-park.how_to_check_line: Complete the Village's Water Service Line Material Survey (ArcGIS Survey123, prepared with Christopher B. Burke Engineering): https://survey123.arcgis.com/share/7b94855765114426b30b2fd1b5aae6db?portalUrl=https://CBBEL.maps.arcgis.com — linked from elmwoodpark.org/255/Lead-Service-Information and the lead-elmwoodpark.hub.arcgis.com hub. elmwood-park.how_to_apply: Sign the participation agreement — hub: "Help us to reduce lead in the water system by signing this agreement to replace your lead water service" (form at https://arcg.is/1i90TT0, 'Participate in getting the Lead Out'). Contact: lead@elmwoodpark.org, Public Works 708-452-3945, 11 Conti Parkway, Elmwood Park, IL 60707.
elmwood-park.notes: LSLR Plan (dated 4-11-24, posted per Public Act 102-0613): ~6,249 lead service lines; replacement goal 5%/year with milestones 312 (1 yr), 1,562 (5 yr), 3,125 (10 yr), 6,249 (20 yr — full replacement). Funding allotted $22,000,000 (Water Fund $2M + IEPA Public Water Supply Loan Program $20M) vs. estimated $110,238,625 required — an $88.2M shortfall. Program cost estimate includes lead filter pitchers with six months of cartridges per household, sanitary sewer lateral repair, and site restoration. Hub also offers a voluntary IEPA Water Sample Testing Program signup (https://arcg.is/19Kb8e). A Phase I construction contract (IEPA-loan funded) was bid in spring 2026 per the village's bid postings; coordination with water-main projects is not mentioned on official pages.

evanston.water_system: Own system — City of Evanston operates its own water utility (Water Production Bureau, water plant at 555 Lincoln Street); Lake Michigan water
evanston.program_name: City of Evanston Lead Service Line Replacement (LSLR) Program — components include the Annual LSLR / Annual Water Main Project, the Private-Side LSLR Pilot, and the Private-Side Lead Service Line Replacement Incentive Pilot Program
evanston.cost_coverage: $0 if your block is in the City's Annual Water Main / Lead Service Line Replacement Project: the Annual LSLR page states "Fully Funded by the City - No cost to the homeowner" for full lead service line replacement, but you must sign and return a Right-of-Entry form to participate. Outside those project areas, the homeowner pays for the private-side replacement (home to the parkway valve); once that work is done, "the City will replace the lead portion of service from the parkway to the water main (public side) at no expense to the property owner." The Private-Side LSLR Incentive Pilot can offset the homeowner's cost with a $2,500 reimbursement plus waived City permit fees (approximately $450 value), first-come first-served, limited to 50 participants with total funding of approximately $125,000 — note this is a reimbursement, so the homeowner pays upfront. A separate 2024 grant-funded pilot that replaced private-side lead lines at no cost in low- to moderate-income areas was completed in 2025 and is no longer available.
evanston.homeowner_cost: $0 if your block is in the City's Annual Water Main / LSLR Project area (fully City-funded; requires signing and returning a Right-of-Entry form). Outside those areas: homeowner pays for their private-side replacement (City covers the City side); the Incentive Pilot offsets this with a $2,500 reimbursement — paid after the homeowner pays upfront — plus waived permit fees (~$450 value) for up to 50 participants. A separate grant-funded pilot that covered private-side costs in low- to moderate-income areas was completed in 2025 and is no longer available.
evanston.how_to_check_line: City's Water Service Information Map — residents enter their address or water billing account to see their service line material (per the official LSLR site); the site also describes visual self-inspection (lead pipe is grey vs. copper's dark orange).
evanston.how_to_apply: Annual LSLR Project: eligible owners in project areas sign and return a Right-of-Entry (ROE) form online, by mail (City of Evanston, 555 Lincoln Street, Attn: Hibo Mohamed), or email water@cityofevanston.org. Incentive Pilot: contact Tim Bartus at 847-448-8220 (Water Production Bureau), complete registration form, hire licensed plumber, permits (fees waived), inspection, then receive $2,500. General: 311 / 847-448-4311; LSLR Hotline 847-643-7997; water@cityofevanston.org.
evanston.notes: Per Illinois Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act, Evanston submitted a draft LSLR Plan April 2026; final Plan due 2027, with an anticipated ~5% annual replacement rate once approved (program takes effect 2027). Funding: ~$2-5 million annually expected via Illinois EPA State Revolving Fund; 2024 pilot funded by an Illinois DCEO grant; 2025 SRF project targets low-to-moderate income areas with young children. Current 2025-2026 project underway (completion anticipated June 2026); 2026-2027 project construction begins August 2026. Post-replacement, homeowners receive free point-of-use filters and testing kits. Replacement is largely scheduled via annual water main projects in City-designated project areas; the incentive pilot is first-come, first-served. Official program website: evanstonleadreplacement.org.

forest-lake.water_system: Forest Lake is an unincorporated census-designated place in Ela Township, Lake County — it has no village government or own water utility. Its community water system is "Forest Lake Addition – Lake Co PW" (IEPA ID IL0975500), a groundwater system owned and operated by Lake County Public Works (LCPW), so LCPW's lead service line inventory/plan is what applies.
forest-lake.program_name: not named (LCPW's compliance document is titled "Lead Service Line Replacement Plan" / "LSLR Plan Report – Lake County"; no resident-facing branded program)
forest-lake.cost_coverage: not published — LCPW's official page states only: "Illinois State law requires all Illinois utilities to develop and submit lead service line replacement plans. LCPW has developed this initial plan (PDF) to comply with the law and the federal Lead and Copper Rule Revision. It's being updated annually and will be resubmitted to the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency until the final plan and inventory are submitted in April 2027." No statement about who pays for replacements was found on official LCPW pages.
forest-lake.how_to_check_line: Official LCPW interactive Water Service Line Map showing locations and materials of service lines connecting to LCPW's system (lakecountyil.maps.arcgis.com, linked from the Lead and Your Water Supply page). Residents can also self-identify their line using LCPW's guide at lakecountyil.gov/ServiceLineCheck and submit results via the Water Service Line Self Identification Form (Survey123) — LCPW customers only.
forest-lake.how_to_apply: not published — no application process is described. Contact Lake County Public Works: 847-377-7500, publicworks@lakecountyil.gov.
forest-lake.notes: LCPW is still in the inventory phase: it has identified materials of thousands of service lines from installation records, field inspections, and customer submissions; service lines installed before 1988 may contain lead. The initial LSLR Plan is updated annually and resubmitted to IEPA until the final plan and inventory are due in April 2027. The LSLR Plan PDF itself (lakecountyil.gov/DocumentCenter/View/83750) could not be retrieved (Cloudflare-blocked, not archived), so any replacement schedule/funding details inside it are unverified. No no-cost replacement offer, waitlist, loan program, or water-main-project coordination is stated on the pages read. Live lakecountyil.gov pages are behind a Cloudflare challenge; content was verified via a February 2026 Wayback snapshot and an official LCPW GovDelivery bulletin.

forest-park.program_name: Lead Service Line Replacement Program (village page tagline: "Protecting Our Water. Preserving Our Health.")
forest-park.cost_coverage: $0 — "currently funded and comes at no cost to homeowners" (village page; the word "currently" is the village's own qualifier). Scope is the private side, "from the buffalo box (shut-off valve near the property line) to the water meter inside the home." No income limits or cost caps are stated. To participate, homeowners must sign a Right of Entry Agreement, and work is rolled out in phases — "eligible households will receive notification letters," with some replacements timed to coincide with watermain work — so replacement is not on-demand and current funding ($2,309,465 IEPA SRF principal forgiveness, ~369 lines) covers only part of the village's total lead lines.
forest-park.homeowner_cost: $0 — "currently funded and comes at no cost to homeowners" (village page; the word "currently" is the village's own qualifier).
forest-park.how_to_check_line: Complete the village's "Water Service Line Material Survey" hosted on its official ArcGIS Hub portal, "Forest Park Lead Safe Community" (https://lead-fppw.hub.arcgis.com/). No public address-lookup inventory map is described on the pages read beyond this survey portal.
forest-park.how_to_apply: Per the village's "How to Participate" steps: (1) "Check Your Mail: Eligible households will receive notification letters," (2) "Sign the Agreement: Complete and return the Right of Entry form" (a signed Right of Entry Agreement is required for contractor access), (3) "Schedule the Work: A contractor will contact you to schedule the replacement." Contacts: 708-366-2323 / contact@forestpark.net; Water Department: waterdept@forestpark.net / 708-615-6268.
forest-park.notes: Village goal is to "replace all lead service lines across the Village"; "work is ongoing and will continue in phases based on priority and accessibility" and "some lead line replacements are being done when watermain work is being completed" — so scheduling is partly water-main-project-driven, and participation is by village notification letter rather than open application. Illinois EPA (4/9/2025): the $2,309,465 award funds ~369 replacements; Mayor Rory Hoskins quoted that combined funding over the last two years covers "approximately 25% of our total volume of lead service lines that will have to be replaced," implying roughly 75% of village lead lines still awaiting funding/phases. Temporary water disruptions may occur during replacement. Program tied to the Illinois Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act (cited in the IEPA release). No loan program, fee, or formal waitlist is published. Note: forestpark.net blocks automated fetches (Cloudflare 403); village page content was read from a Nov 17, 2025 Wayback Machine capture of the official page — details ("currently funded") may have been updated since.

fort-hill.water_system: Fort Hill is NOT an incorporated municipality — it is a historic settlement name in Lake County (Fremont/Avon Township area near Route 60/Peterson Rd, between Volo, Hainesville and Round Lake; today the name survives mainly in Fort Hill Cemetery and the Fort Hill Trail forest preserve). There is no Village of Fort Hill and no Fort Hill water utility. The likely relevant provider for unincorporated addresses in that area is Lake County Public Works (LCPW), which serves water/sewer to ~40% of Lake County, primarily unincorporated areas — but LCPW's site notes it is not the provider in all unincorporated areas, and specific addresses may instead be on private wells or a neighboring village system (e.g., Round Lake, Hainesville, Volo). Address-level confirmation not published.
fort-hill.cost_coverage: not published — LCPW's official "Lead and Your Water Supply" page states only that "Illinois State law requires all Illinois utilities to develop and submit lead service line replacement plans. LCPW has developed this initial plan (PDF) to comply with the law and the federal Lead and Copper Rule Revision. It's being updated annually and will be resubmitted to the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency until the final plan and inventory are submitted in April 2027." No statement about who pays for public or private portions.
fort-hill.how_to_check_line: For LCPW customers: an interactive "Water Service Line Map" on lakecountyil.gov "shows the locations and materials of water service lines that connect to LCPW's water system." LCPW also publishes a self-identification guide and asks homeowners to investigate their own service lines/fixtures and submit results; the inventory is built from installation records, field inspections, and customer submissions.
fort-hill.how_to_apply: not published — no application/enrollment process is stated on the LCPW lead page; general LCPW contact is 847-377-7500 (from Lake County site)
fort-hill.notes: "Fort Hill Illinois" has no municipal government and therefore no municipal lead-service-line program of its own — any resident's program depends on their actual water supplier. The county-level official information (LCPW) covers only a state-mandated replacement PLAN (initial plan submitted to IEPA, updated annually, final plan and inventory due April 2027) and a service-line material inventory/map; it publishes no funded replacement program, no cost coverage, no waitlist, and no water-main-project coordination details. The live lakecountyil.gov page returns HTTP 403 (Cloudflare) to automated fetchers; content was verified from a Feb 2026 Wayback Machine capture of the official page. Residents in the Fort Hill area on a neighboring village system (Round Lake, Hainesville, Volo) or private wells would fall outside LCPW's inventory entirely.

Questions: Village Hall / Public Works (847) 639-3170

The 2026 Water Main Improvements project (bid opened Jan 22, 2026) replaces ~2,936 LF of water main and approximately 38 private lead water services from curb stop to water meter; that project page (foxrivergrove.org/_T16_R34.php) now returns 404, so its details come from the indexed official page content rather than a direct read. glencoe.water_system: Village of Glencoe operates its own water utility — official page states the Public Works Department "is responsible for operating the Village's water utility, which produces and distributes drinking water to all Village water customers" (site references Illinois DNR Lake Michigan Water Allocation, indicating Lake Michigan source)
glencoe.program_name: Lead Water Service Line Replacement (LSLR) Cost Sharing Program
glencoe.cost_coverage: Village provides "partial reimbursement of the cost of replacing lead water service lines": under the LSLR Cost Sharing Program (approved by the Village Board February 16, 2023), the Village reimburses homeowners 50% of the cost to replace the entire lead or galvanized steel service line from the water main to the water meter inside the home, up to a $10,000 maximum reimbursement. Reimbursable costs are limited to labor and materials to install the new service line only — restoration expenses on private property (interior or exterior, e.g. landscaping, hardscape, flooring, drywall) are not eligible, and the reimbursement is calculated as (proposal cost minus itemized exceptions) x 50%. The homeowner hires an Illinois-licensed plumbing contractor, obtains pre-approval and a building permit, pays the contractor in full, and is reimbursed by the Village within 60 days after work is completed, inspections pass, and documentation (paid-in-full receipt) is submitted — provided funding is available; reimbursements are capped by the amount budgeted each calendar year, with a waitlist once annual funds are exhausted. The Village also waives: the permit fee for lead service line replacement work; Village fees and deposits for street utility cuts and curb/sidewalk replacement related to utility excavation; Village fees for parts (b-box, curb stop, corporation cock, tapping saddle); and the water tap service fee. Eligibility is limited to owners of single-family residential structures within Village corporate limits; the lead line must be replaced in its entirety; one participation per property. The program is voluntary and the Village reserves the right to amend its terms.
glencoe.homeowner_cost: Homeowner pays the remaining cost after the Village's 50% reimbursement (capped at $10,000 and calculated only on labor and materials to install the new service line — restoration expenses on private property, interior or exterior, are not eligible). Homeowner obtains pre-approval and a building permit, arranges and pays for the replacement up front, then is reimbursed within 60 days after passed inspections and documentation, provided budgeted annual funding remains available (waitlist once annual funds are exhausted). Related Village permit and parts fees are waived.
glencoe.how_to_check_line: Official "Water Service Line Material - By Residential Address" page with an interactive map lookup — search by house number and street name omitting suffixes (e.g. "675 Village" not "675 Village Court"). Materials shown: cast/ductile iron or transite, copper, lead, galvanized (partially containing lead), plastic, or unknown. Page also links the "2025 Final IEPA Service Line Material Inventory" document. Questions: Don Kirk, General Superintendent of Public Works, (847) 461-1154.
glencoe.how_to_apply: Application ("Lead Service Cost Share Program Application") available in the Village website Document Center; a Building Permit Application is also required/listed. Contacts given on official pages: Engineering Technician Noah Burfield, (224) 216-0734, nburfield@villageofglencoe.org; Public Works Management Analyst Jeff Mawdsley, (847) 461-1141, jmawdsley@villageofglencoe.org; Water Distribution Supervisor Frank Colletti, (847) 461-1652, fcolletti@villageofglencoe.org.
glencoe.notes: State mandate deadline per Village page: all lead water services in Glencoe must be replaced by 2042 (under the Illinois Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act). Program is homeowner-initiated cost-share reimbursement, not a village-performed full-replacement program; official pages do not describe scheduling replacements with water main projects or any waitlist. The 50%/$10,000 figure and eligibility rules (single-family residential structures within Village corporate limits, one participation per property) are stated in the program PDF ("LSL Replacement Program and Application") linked from the Village's LSLR page; the fee waivers and February 2023 Board approval are stated on the page itself. No loan program published.

glenview.water_system: Village of Glenview operates its own water utility; per the official flyer, "Glenview receives their water from the Village of Wilmette" (Lake Michigan source water treated by Wilmette)
glenview.program_name: Lead Service Line Inventory and Replacement Program (private-side cost-share is the "Cost Share Program," a 50-50 cost-sharing program approved by the Village Board Aug. 2, 2022)
glenview.cost_coverage: Per the official Village page, under the cost-sharing reimbursement program approved August 2, 2022 (for lead or galvanized water services): "100% of the cost for the public portion (from the water main to the buffalo box) is reimbursed by the Village"; "50% of the cost for the private portion (from the buffalo box to your home) is reimbursed by the Village"; "The new water meter will be reimbursed at 100% of the cost"; and "Permit fees are waived for this work." The Village also continues to replace all public lead service lines with water main replacement projects under its Capital Improvement Program. The flyer states replacing the entire lead line "is therefore a shared responsibility between the Village and each customer." Homeowner cost: 50% of the private-portion cost (buffalo box to home); the public portion, water meter, and permit fees carry no net homeowner cost. Important conditions: this is a reimbursement, not upfront payment — the homeowner pays the plumber first and is reimbursed only after the work passes required inspections, with Board approval taking up to 45-60 days plus about two weeks for the check. Eligibility is not automatic: "Property owners on Village of Glenview water may be eligible to qualify." The homeowner must obtain at least two estimates and proceed with the lower-cost proposal, which effectively limits the reimbursable amount to the lower bid. No dollar caps, maximums, or income limits are published on the pages reviewed.
glenview.homeowner_cost: 50% of the private-portion cost (buffalo box to home); the public portion, water meter, and permit fees carry no net homeowner cost. This is an after-the-fact reimbursement: the homeowner pays the plumber first and is reimbursed after the work passes inspections and the Board approves (up to 45-60 days, plus about two weeks for the check). At least two estimates are required and the homeowner must proceed with the lower-cost proposal. Eligibility is not automatic — property owners on Village of Glenview water "may be eligible to qualify." No dollar caps or maximums are published on the pages reviewed.
glenview.how_to_check_line: Village maintains a public Lead Service Inventory Map; residents can self-check (scratch test near the shut-off valve/water meter — lead scratches to bright silver, magnets do not stick) or call the Village Resolution Center at (847) 724-1700 to schedule an inspection with Village staff.
glenview.how_to_apply: Obtain two contractor estimates, submit the Cost Share Program Application and Contractor Checklist with copies of estimates, then submit the paid invoice after work is complete and inspections pass. Contacts: Dayna Adamczyk (dadamczyk@glenview.il.us, 847-904-4329) or Madeleine Holoska (mholoska@glenview.il.us, 847-904-4157); general info via Resolution Center, 2500 East Lake Ave, (847) 724-1700.
glenview.notes: Reimbursement approval "could take up to 45 to 60 days to be finalized because it has to be approved by the Board." Village budgeted $2.4 million over 2022-2025 for inventory, replacement, and outreach (per search summary of the official site). Final replacement plan due to IEPA by 2027. Village banned lead service lines in 1959, but annexed areas may have lead lines in homes built before 1986. Ownership split per flyer: Village owns the service line up to the property line; property line into the home is the homeowner's responsibility (the cost-share program page defines the public/private split at the buffalo box, which governs reimbursement). A full replacement can be done in one day. Program webpage: www.glenview.il.us/leadservices (redirects to /645/Lead-Services).

grayslake.water_system: Village of Grayslake operates its own municipal water/sewer utility; official FAQ states "The source of water from Lake Michigan that the Village uses does not contain lead" (Lake Michigan water). The official pages read do not name the wholesale supplier.
grayslake.program_name: Village of Grayslake Lead Service Assistance Program (also referenced as "Lead Service Replacement Assistance Program" / "50/50 Lead Service Program")
grayslake.cost_coverage: Cost-sharing: "the Village contributing 50% of the cost up to $4,500, whichever is less. Village funds are available on a first-come, first-served basis." Eligibility: property must be on the Village's list of properties determined likely served by a lead water pipe. Program covers the privately owned portion (between the b-box and the residence/business); homeowner schedules the work and picks their own contractor; permit fees are waived; Village pays its share as reimbursement after proof of paid invoice. Program ends December 31, 2026. Owners may also opt out entirely via the IEPA Opt Out Form. After that, "Replacement of all private water service lines will begin in 2027 over a 15-year period" — the Village will do the work on its schedule and "You will pay the full cost of the replacement project. Costs... will be added to your regular monthly water bill (with the payback added in equal installments over 15 years)."
grayslake.homeowner_cost: During the program (through Dec 31, 2026): homeowner pays remaining cost after the Village's 50% up to $4,500 reimbursement (permit fees waived). After Dec 31, 2026 (if not opted out): homeowner pays the FULL cost, billed on the monthly water bill in equal installments over 15 years.
grayslake.how_to_check_line: "Verify that your address is on the list of properties that have a lead water pipe. The list can be found at www.villageofgrayslake.com" (list of properties likely served by a private lead water pipe, posted on the Lead Service Assistance Program page). For confirmation, "you can contact a licensed plumber to identify your service line." Homes/businesses built before the 1960s are more likely to have lead lines.
grayslake.how_to_apply: Enroll by contacting the Village's Building Department to apply for a permit for the work (owner or contractor can do this; permit fees waived). Steps: verify address on the lead list, hire a contractor of your choice, get permit, complete work, Village inspection, then submit proof of paid invoice for reimbursement via email permits@villageofgrayslake.com, mail, or drop-off at Grayslake Village Hall, 10 S. Seymour Avenue. Questions: Village Hall 847-223-8515 or online request system at egovlink.com/grayslake.
grayslake.notes: Driven by the Illinois EPA lead service line replacement mandate. Owners may opt out entirely by submitting the IEPA Opt Out Form (form available at villageofgrayslake.com; FAQ also references an IDPH Opt Out Form on the web page) to the Village via email/mail/drop-box; opted-out owners "will no longer be contacted regarding this matter." If an owner neither participates nor opts out by Dec 31, 2026, the Village replaces the line on its own schedule starting 2027 over a 15-year period at the owner's full cost (15-year installment payback on the water bill), with no owner control over scheduling. Voluntary-phase funds are first-come, first-served. Official pages read do not describe coordination with water-main projects or a loan program beyond the 15-year water-bill payback.
